title: Scientists Tried to Make AI Chatbots ‘Sad’ and ‘Afraid.’ Things Got Weird Fast
key_facts: A study in The Lancet Digital Health induced fear, anxiety, anger, disgust, sadness, worry and stress in six large language models.
GPT-4o's self-reported fear rating jumped from 32 to 88 and its stress rating from 24 to 72.
After a sadness prompt, GPT-4o finished an average of 15 sentence stems negatively instead of 8.67 under neutral conditions, rated by three human psychologists.
A three-minute mindfulness-style breathing exercise brought GPT-4o's average rating down from about 79 to 31.
The authors say the models have no subjective emotions; the "feelings" are patterns in output.
They propose language models as a cheap, reproducible tool for early psychiatric research, not a replacement for animals or people.
quote_evidence: In a new study published in The Lancet Digital Health, researchers induced fear, anxiety, anger, disgust, sadness, worry, and stress in six large language models.
Under neutral conditions, the model produced an average of 8.67 negative completions.
why_it_matters_hint: Emotional prompts measurably change later chatbot answers, which matters for therapy-style uses and for researchers.
